title: Choose the portfolio's visual world
question: Which world makes design judgment and engineering depth feel like one senior practice?

options.label: The Release Ledger
options.lineage: software release binders, QA sign-off sheets, and physical change-control records
options.thesis: Four shipped products become release records that expose decisions, systems, and proof side by side.
options.viewport: An oversized blue release sheet fills the screen; Ivaylo's role, four project tabs, and a DESIGNED / ENGINEERED comparison rail are embedded into the document.
options.risk: Can feel procedural unless large product imagery interrupts the ledger at decisive moments.

raised.raise: Transitions gain one confident physical snap instead of generic fades.
Every dense record earns a composed clearing around its central artifact.
Design, system, and shipping proof stay visibly layered without relying on gradients.
Interaction states announce themselves inside the record instead of hiding in decorative chrome.

options.label: Product Anatomy Atlas
options.lineage: industrial cutaway manuals and exploded product diagrams
options.thesis: Each project is opened into experience, system, and shipping layers so seniority is visible without being claimed.
options.viewport: A huge exploded project stack occupies two-thirds of the screen, separating a real UI surface, its system diagram, and deployment evidence along one draggable axis.
options.risk: The strongest and clearest fit, but cutaway portfolios are more familiar than the rolled direction.

options.label: Color Chord Canopy
options.lineage: tensioned translucent banners crossing a bright courtyard
options.thesis: Design and engineering are independent color bands whose overlap reveals the finished product.
options.viewport: Wide translucent lanes cross over live project imagery; soloing DESIGN or ENGINEERING changes the evidence, while the overlap shows the shipped whole.
options.case: Product clarity is excellent because the overlap performs the portfolio's premise; hiring-context identification is weaker than the ledger.
options.risk: Requires disciplined type and real imagery or it becomes an abstract art demo.

options.label: The Maker Stack
options.lineage: HyperCard stacks where reading and making share the same object
options.thesis: The portfolio is a stack of project cards that visitors can inspect in browse mode and peel open in maker mode.
options.viewport: One oversized project card shows the live product; a MAKER MODE control reveals decisions, component anatomy, and implementation notes in place.
options.case: Digital makers identify with it immediately; the retro language risks understating the maturity of the work.
options.risk: Can read as nostalgic novelty unless scale, spacing, and typography are ruthlessly contemporary.

options.label: Animated Studio Reel
options.thesis: Projects arrive as rhythmic animated scenes in a maker's reel.
options.viewport: A circular iris opens onto the first shipped product as a short visual gag.
options.case: It weakens both hiring identification and product clarity by turning serious work into entertainment.
options.kept: One decisive motion beat can make state changes memorable without becoming playful everywhere.
options.risk: The form overwhelms the evidence and makes senior work feel whimsical.

options.label: The Living Margin
options.thesis: Project evidence sits in clearings cut from a living ornamental frame.
options.viewport: A precise growing border frames one calm project statement and a single screen artifact.
options.case: The craft is visible, but employers must work too hard to connect the ornament to product practice.
options.kept: Dense evidence should always open into a deliberate visual clearing.
options.risk: Feels like an illustrator's portfolio rather than a product designer-developer's body of work.

options.label: Layered Product Roundel
options.thesis: Every product gains depth from separately cut design and engineering layers.
options.viewport: A symmetrical layered project medallion assembles around a central interface capture.
options.case: The layer metaphor is clear, but the folk-craft identity distracts from the professional hiring context.
options.kept: Depth must come from structural overlap rather than glass effects or ornamental gradients.
options.risk: The page could feel decorative and culturally borrowed rather than personally grounded.

options.label: The Shipping Transcript
options.thesis: A live transcript prints each project's decisions and system states as evidence.
options.viewport: A continuous release transcript opens with the latest project and keyboard-first navigation.
options.case: Developers identify with it, but it collapses the design half of the portfolio into a coder cliché.
options.kept: Important states should print their meaning instead of relying on ambiguous decorative cues.
options.risk: It is exactly the neon-terminal portfolio rut this redesign must avoid.

canonCard.label: Contemporary case-study portfolio
canonCard.thesis: A clear modern portfolio with a restrained grid, large screenshots, concise case studies, and a direct hiring path.
canonCard.viewport: A concise introduction sits beside one large featured-project frame, followed by a straightforward selected-work index.
canonCard.risk: Highly legible and employable, but intentionally difficult to distinguish from other polished portfolios.
